title: Tractional & Exudative Retinal Detachment: Pathogenesis, Diagnosis, and Management
summary: An exhaustive clinical guide to the mechanisms, diagnostic signs, and treatment modalities for non-rhegmatogenous retinal detachments, specifically focusing on the progressive contraction of fibrovascular membranes and the accumulation of subretinal fluid.

sections.title: Pathogenesis of Diabetic TRD
content: 1. Progressive contraction of fibrovascular membranes occurs over large areas of vitreoretinal adhesion.
2. Gradual and frequently incomplete PVD (unlike acute PVD in rhegmatogenous RD).
3. Leakage of plasma constituents into the vitreous gel from fibrovascular networks adherent to the posterior vitreous surface.
4. Cortical vitreous remains strongly adherent to areas of fibrovascular proliferation.
5. Rare Event: If a subsequent complete PVD occurs, new blood vessels are avulsed and RD does not develop.

sections.title: The Mechanics of Vitreoretinal Traction
content: Tangential Traction: Caused by contraction of epiretinal fibrovascular membranes; results in puckering of the retina and distortion of blood vessels.
Anteroposterior Traction: Due to contraction of fibrovascular membranes extending from the posterior retina (usually major arcades) to the vitreous base anteriorly and/or bridging (trampoline).
Bridge Traction: Contraction of fibrovascular membranes stretching from one part of the retina to another or between vascular arcades, pulling the two involved points together.

sections.title: TRD Clinical Indicators & B-Scan
content: B-scan ultrasonography shows incomplete PVD and a relatively immobile retina (Fig. 16.34B).
Signs (Fig. 16.34A): Localized tractional detachment secondary to preretinal fibrosis.
Combined Tractional–Rhegmatogenous RD: If a break occurs, it assumes rhegmatogenous characteristics and progresses rapidly.

sections.title: Exudative Retinal Detachment (ERD) Pathogenesis
sections.content: Exudative RD is characterized by the accumulation of SRF in the absence of retinal breaks or traction. It occurs in vascular, inflammatory, and neoplastic diseases involving the retina, RPE, and choroid. Fluid leaks outside vessels and accumulates under the retina. While the RPE can normally pump leaking fluid into choroidal circulation, RD occurs when this mechanism is overwhelmed or functions sub-normally.

sections.title: Etiology of Exudative Retinal Detachment
content: Choroidal tumours: Melanoma, haemangioma, and metastases.
Inflammation: Harada disease and posterior scleritis.
Bullous central serous chorioretinopathy (rare cause).
Iatrogenic: RD surgery and panretinal photocoagulation.
Choroidal neovascularization: Extensive subretinal fluid at the posterior pole.
Hypertensive choroidopathy: E.g., toxaemia of pregnancy (very rare).
Idiopathic: Uveal effusion syndrome.

sections.title: CRITICAL TIP: Tumor Warning
content: An intraocular tumour should be considered the cause of an exudative RD until proved otherwise.
Exudative RD is characterized by 'shifting' subretinal fluid.

sections.title: The 'Shifting Fluid' Phenomenon
content: 1. Gravity-Dependent: SRF detaches the area of retina under which it accumulates (Fig. 16.35A/B).
2. Upright Position: SRF collects under the inferior retina.
3. Supine Position: After several minutes, the inferior retina flattens.
4. Posterior Shift: SRF shifts posteriorly, detaching the superior retina.

sections.title: Additional ERD Signs & Diagnostics
content: Bilateral Involvement: Depending on the cause, both eyes may be involved simultaneously.
Systemic Association: Patients may have systemic disease responsible (e.g., Harada disease, toxaemia of pregnancy).
Leopard Spots: Consist of scattered areas of subretinal pigment clumping seen after the detachment has flattened (Fig. 16.36B).
Visual Evidence: Choroidal tumours may be apparent on fundus exam or B-scan (Fig. 16.36A).

sections.title: Treatment Strategies for ERD
content: Cause-Dependent: Treatment is tailored to the specific underlying etiology.
Spontaneous Resolution: Some cases resolve without intervention.
Systemic Corticosteroids: Used for inflammatory causes like Harada disease and posterior scleritis.
Laser Photocoagulation: Used to seal the leak in the RPE in some eyes with bullous central serous chorioretinopathy.
